analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to send all environmental testing to private laboratories instead of government labs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote; it sat in five House subcommittees until the 1996 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced every federal agency doing environmental testing — checking water, air, and soil for pollution monitoring and for enforcing environmental laws — to stop using government labs and buy that work exclusively from private laboratories. It also would have applied to states, local governments, and universities that do such testing using federal grant money. It never moved past its committee referrals and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Private environmental testing laboratories would gain a captive market: every federal agency, and any state, local, or university lab using federal grant money, would be required to purchase their testing services from commercial labs. Federal, state, and university labs would lose this work.

how_it_helps.text: Requires all federal departments and agencies doing environmental testing for monitoring, assessment, or compliance decisions to use exclusively nongovernmental laboratories, so long as testing protocols, method requirements, and sample handling times can still be met.
Extends the same requirement to state and local governments and colleges performing environmental testing with federal grant money, expanding the mandate beyond the federal government itself.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would bear any extra cost of contracting out work currently done in-house, and the federal, state, and university laboratories that now perform this testing would lose their role — including the loss of in-house scientific capability built for oversight of environmental laws.

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate in-house government laboratory capability for environmental monitoring and enforcement, leaving agencies dependent on outside contractors for the science behind their own compliance decisions.

It applies to states, localities, and universities using federal assistance, which could force closure or downsizing of public and academic environmental labs and disrupt existing testing arrangements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill creates a guaranteed market for private labs, but the public benefit is not demonstrated: it does not show that commercial testing is cheaper or better, while it strips agencies and universities of independent in-house testing capacity used for monitoring and enforcement. Any savings would depend entirely on private lab pricing, and the loss of public-sector scientific capability would be permanent.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then split among five subcommittees, none of which acted on it, and it died when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. William Lipinski introduced the bill on August 1, 1995, for himself and Rep. David Poshard, and it was sent to the House Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Natural Resources Committees.

On August 14, 1995, it was referred to five subcommittees — Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials; Health and Environment; Energy and Power; Water Resources and Environment; and Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation — and no further action was ever taken.
The bill attracted three cosponsors (one Democrat and two Republicans) in addition to the original sponsors, but never received a committee vote or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal, state, and university environmental labs kept their work, and taxpayers avoided a mandated shift to contracted testing whose cost and quality were unproven. The bill's sponsors and the private labs it would have benefited gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. William O. Lipinski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require exclusive use of private laboratories for environmental testing.

for.name: Rep. David Poshard
for.what_they_did: Joined Lipinski in introducing the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but thin — a Democratic sponsor with one Democratic and two Republican cosponsors — and no votes were ever recorded on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have handed commercial labs a legal monopoly on environmental testing for federal agencies and for any state, local, or university lab using federal money. Their gain would come at public expense, with no showing that contracted testing is cheaper or better than in-house work.

Federal labs and state, local, and academic labs doing federally funded testing would lose the work, threatening their continued operation. Their in-house testing supports environmental monitoring and enforcement that protects the public.
